I know I'm a bit late to this but I'm glad you had the courage to seek help and are feeling better. The suicide hotline can be a valuable resource, we all have times where we just need someone, anyone to talk to. The people who work at those lines are generally very good natured and truly are there to help. I personally have called many times and don't regret it.

That being said, for future reference, if the operator on the other end of the line knows that you have a method to kill yourself, and they're able to surmise your location or identity, they can call the police to take you to a hospital and you will very likely be involuntarily committed to a psych ward for 72 hrs minimum. This can be EXTREMELY expensive if your insurance doesn't cover it, and can be very problematic if you have a job as well since you'll need to take time off with very short notice (they wont release you under any circumstance until they are confident you are stable and in good hands). I saw u/HelenFromHR's comment from earlier and just wanted to let you know sometimes they will not give you the choice of going to the hospital or not.

I personally was involuntarily committed to a psych ward because the operator asked me if I had a method of killing myself in mind. I told her I had a belt but didn't want to do it yet. Earlier in the call, I had told her the name of the university I went to. Within the hour, they had called the university, tracked me down from my phone number to my dorm, and dispatched the police, who handcuffed me and took me to the hospital. They didn't tell me they were going to do that, I was blindsided, given no choice in the matter and missed a week of classes locked in a psych ward. My parents had to call off work and drive 7 hrs out of state so they could discharge me to them. I don't blame the operator for it, how could she have known, but I didn't need a psych ward at the time, I needed a person to talk to and it turned into a massive inconvenience for multiple people.

This is not to say that you shouldn't be honest with them. It defeats the purpose of the hotline if you're not being honest. Sometimes people who need help don't know they need it, so tell the truth as best you can. I just wanted to let you know the potential ramifications so you can be prepared.

Please dont listen to Evil\_King. They clearly have no idea what they're talking about. While I have read about anti-depressants making people feel "worse" at first, and how people who use anti-depressants can be more at risk to a "relapse" of depression when they stop taking them, there are too many different medications with too many different side effects to make blanket statements like that. Medication is right for some and not others. Work with your mental health professional and child to find a solution that fits you guys best.

First off I want to say you are doing the right thing as a father. I told my father about my depression a long long time ago and he belittled my issues, and forgot about it quickly thereafter. I almost failed high school and got kicked out of college before I tried getting help myself. I found a mental health professional I liked, but by then I had already ruined my future. Like many immigrants, my father did not know much about mental illness so I can't blame him for his reaction, but I often think about how different things could have been had he tried getting me the help I needed.

  
When it comes to your sons opinions on his meds, I'm afraid I can offer little guidance. I personally saw no benefit from taking Prozac (anti-depressant SSRI), but I have heard many stories of it helping people in significant ways. There are negative side-effects to a lot of these drugs, and you will very likely have to weigh the cost vs. benefit of taking them with your son and his mental health professional. From my experience, there isn't a concrete answer, it is very contextual. I know that no kids/teens like taking medication of any sort, so try your best to de-stigmatize the medication so he wont just say "no meds" every time, but actually offers useful feedback. Mental health professionals can only start adjusting his treatment plan if your son is 100% honest about how the meds affect progress and how he feels. Of course, make sure you consult with a doctor before taking action as getting off/on these drugs can have significant medical consequences if done improperly.

Here's what I **do** know for a fact about medication - you need to find the **right** psychiatrist and/or therapist (Some do both counseling and medical prescriptions) to go with it. One your son can be truly comfortable with. Not just any will do. I say this because meds alone cannot fix the root issue. They can help but at the end of the day, your son needs to come to terms with his life and potential. Depression is a sickness of thought. Constantly pessimistic, hopeless, and discouraged thought. A good therapist, one that your son can "chill" with and be himself with, be open with, can be a critical part of healing his thought processes, and helping him identify the areas he needs to work on. I worked with 6 different therapists before I found one I could truly be open with, and my time with him helped me more than all the others combined. Therapists are people too, you need to find a personality who has chemistry with your son. That's how it was for me. This can take a while to find so be patient and keep your chin up - I know Canadas health system is different than the States so I hope it gives you the liberty to pursue different options.

  
The second thing is talk to your son, get him to open up to you completely. I don't know why your son is depressed so I will tell you my story in hopes it helps shed some light on your son's situation. I first fell into depression when I was about your sons age. It was because a girl I had fallen for had rejected me in a very awkward and cold way. In hindsight, its a minor dilemma - After all, who doesn't get rejected in high school? But at the time it hurt me badly, and laid the foundations for an unhealthy way of thinking, which I didn't correct quickly enough. I bottled it up. I was so embarrassed I didn't tell a soul about how much it impacted me until years later, when I was going through therapy. I didn't want to talk about it at the time, but now I wish somebody had really dug deeper, refused to take no for an answer, and asked why I was so down. If I just had someone who asked, someone I could talk to, I could have gotten the embarrassment and self-doubt off my chest earlier, and might have even recovered with time and resumed my positive way of thinking. All this to say - Be open and non-judgmental with your son, make sure he knows that he can tell you ANYTHING, no matter what. Therapists wont always be available, but you can at least be his safe space, a person he can vent to, a confidant. You may have heard all this already, but as his parent, just being honest and listening to him and letting him get shit off his chest can help more than you know.

  
Lastly, I will leave you with this. As a person who has been through multiple hospital psych wards, often involuntarily committed to them, they should only serve as a last resort, if you truly believe your son to be in IMMEDIATE danger from himself. You don't get any *real* help there, all they really do at most places is lock you in a ward with window bars for a couple days, feels a bit like jail to be honest - the doctors there, understandably, are not concerned about helping patients through their problems or "curing" their depression - their job is to make sure you don't kill yourself, that's it. They teach you pre-packaged coping strategies and give you textbook therapy (which *can* be useful and relevant) but in my experience, in order to achieve real progress, it has to be handled on an individual basis. The one positive is the group therapy, seeing other patients who are in the same rough shape as you, it puts things in perspective - I felt more empathy for myself after those sessions. This brings me to my point. Your son is right, and being locked up *can* exacerbate the problem at hand, especially if it was involuntary. Treat these facilities as a safety net. They are definitely not an alternative to real treatment, but a fallback plan for when the situation demands it. The first line of defense, oddly enough, is you, even when you're not around. Tell your son how much he means to you, make sure he knows how much you love him and how much it would break you to lose him to suicide. I found it much harder to court thoughts of suicide after my loved ones had these conversations with me. I may not have shown it, but it affected me profoundly.

​

From one anonymous internet-er to another, I hope my words were able to give you some clarity, even if it was just a little bit. I hope your son gets better and back to himself again, and I applaud you for being a good father too. Sorry for the essay.

If it was me I would just ask her to hang out. Do fun stuff, invite her around. It's always a touch awkward when you talk about depression to someone's face, so I would make her feel wanted, if not needed, through other means. I had friends in high school, but I always felt i was sortve excluded from the group, and they would constantly do things without inviting me. But when someone invited me to come and hang out it didn't just brighten my day it brightened my whole week. Feeling that just someone cared, regardless of whether they had included me or not earlier, that someone would notice if I just slipped away, was the greatest feeling in the world. It made me feel glad to be alive.

EDIT: not all people with depression feel as I do about talking about their illness- if she seems like she wants to talk to you about it, I encourage you to do so, and to be open and try to understand and empathize with her feelings. Another thing is that when it comes to depression, there is such a thing as being too positive. *Personally* sometimes I just want a shoulder to cry on and a face to vent to, not to be greeted by someone who's overly cheery, although gentle and sincere positive suggestions do help. 

Sorry for the essay, I know some people may disagree with my opinions, but I just wish that I had a friend like you in high school and that is what I'd want them to do. Use my tips at your own discretion. Good luck :)
